quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on what a double cloth is, its four thread systems and the rule that keeps the layers apart.

questions.q: How many sets of threads does a double cloth contain?
options: Two: one warp and one weft
Three: two warps and one weft
Four: face warp, face weft, back warp and back weft
questions.explain: A double cloth has a top (face) warp and weft and a bottom (back) warp and weft, four systems in all.

questions.q: What is the one rule that keeps the two layers of a double cloth separate?
options: Every face end is lifted on every back pick, and no back end is lifted on a face pick
Every back end is lifted on every face pick
Face and back ends are lifted together on every pick
The face weft must be coarser than the back weft
questions.explain: The face layer must sit wholly above the back weft and the back layer wholly below the face weft; the rule states exactly this.

questions.q: What does a double cloth become if it is woven with no stitching points at all?
options: A plain weave of double sett
A tube or a bag, two separate cloths joined only at the edges or not at all
questions.explain: Without stitching the layers are unconnected, giving a tube or bag; stitching ties them into one thick cloth.

questions.q: Which of these is a stitching point as described in the lecture?
options: A face end lifted on a face pick
A back end left down on a back pick
A back end lifted over a face pick
A face end lifted on a back pick
questions.explain: Stitching is a back end lifted over a face pick, or a face end dropped under a back pick; a face end up on a back pick is the ordinary separating lift.

questions.q: In the lecture's drawings the ends alternate face, back, face, back, and the picks alternate in the same way.
questions.explain: The drawings use a 1:1 arrangement of face (T) and back (B) threads in both directions.

questions.q: On the lecture's point paper, what do the orange squares show?
options: Face ends lifted out of the way on back picks
questions.explain: Dark squares are each layer's own weave; orange squares are the face ends lifted on back picks to keep the layers apart.

questions.q: What does 'self-stitched' mean for a double cloth?
options: The weft is knotted at the selvedge
The layers are tied together by their own face or back threads, without extra stitching threads
The two cloths are sewn together after weaving
The face cloth stitches itself into a tube
questions.explain: Self-stitching uses the cloth's own ends or picks (a back end over a face pick, or a face end under a back pick) to tie the layers.

questions.q: Within each layer of a double cloth, how do the threads interlace?
options: Always in the same weave as the other layer
They do not interlace within a layer
In their own weave, such as plain or 3/1 twill
questions.explain: Each layer weaves its own structure; the lecture shows plain/plain, plain/3-1 twill, plain/2-1 twill and 3/1 twill in both layers.

questions.q: Why does the lecture say a stitch should be placed between two face ends that are also lifted?
options: So the back weft can pass
So the face warp on either side hides the stitching back end
questions.explain: A back end lifted on a face pick would show on the face unless the neighbouring face ends are up to cover it.

questions.q: A double cloth is chosen when a thin, light cloth is wanted.
questions.explain: Stitched double cloths are thick and bulky; two layers add weight and substance, which is the reason for using them.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: Reading face and back picks, counting lifts, healds and repeat sizes for double cloths.

questions.q: On a face pick row of a 1:1 double-cloth design, which ends are lifted?
options: All the back ends plus the face weave
Only the face ends required by the face weave
questions.explain: On a face pick only face ends lift, following the face weave; the back ends stay down so the face weft passes over them all.

questions.q: On a back pick row, which ends are lifted?
options: Only the back ends of the back weave
Every face end, plus the back ends required by the back weave
questions.explain: The face ends are all lifted out of the way; the back ends then follow the back weave beneath them.

questions.q: With a 1:1 arrangement, how is the minimum ends-repeat of a double cloth found from the two layer weaves?
options: Twice the lowest common multiple of the two layer repeats
The sum of the two layer repeats
The product of the two layer repeats
The larger of the two layer repeats
questions.explain: Each layer must complete whole repeats, so the layer repeat is the LCM; with ends alternating 1:1 the design needs twice that number of ends.

questions.q: A double cloth has a plain face (2-end repeat) and a 2/1 twill back (3-end repeat), ends 1:1. What is its minimum ends-repeat?
questions.explain: LCM of 2 and 3 is 6 threads per layer; two layers 1:1 give 12 ends, matching the lecture's 12 × 12 design.

questions.q: If both layers are plain weave in a 1:1 double cloth, the design repeats on 8 ends and 8 picks.
questions.explain: Plain repeats on 2 threads per layer; interleaving two layers makes 4, and the lecture's plain/plain design is drawn on 8 × 8, two full repeats of the 4 × 4 minimum, so 8 × 8 certainly repeats.

questions.q: How many healds are needed for a self-stitched plain/plain double cloth drafted on a straight draft?
questions.explain: Each plain layer needs 2 healds; the two layers interlace independently, so 2 + 2 = 4.

questions.q: A plain-face, 3/1-twill-back double cloth is drafted straight. How many healds?
questions.explain: Plain needs 2 healds and a 3/1 twill needs 4; 2 + 4 = 6.

questions.q: A double cloth with 40 face ends and 40 back ends per inch has how many ends per inch in the reed?
questions.explain: Both warps are in the same reed, so the total sett is 40 + 40 = 80 ends per inch.

questions.q: Adding stitching points changes the one rule: some face ends are left down on back picks or some back ends are raised on face picks.
questions.explain: A stitch is precisely an exception to the separating rule at chosen points; the rule holds everywhere else.

questions.q: As the number of stitching points per repeat rises, the double cloth becomes…
options: thinner with no change in firmness
firmer and more closely bound, but the stitches risk showing
questions.explain: More ties bind the layers more firmly; too many or badly placed ties show on the face.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Counting lifts, healds, repeats and hex digits on the lecture's double-cloth designs.

questions.q: In the 8-end plain/plain double cloth, a back pick lifts all four face ends and two of the four back ends. How many of the eight ends are lifted on that pick?
questions.explain: 4 face ends + 2 back ends = 6 of the 8 ends are up on a back pick.

questions.q: On a face pick of the same 8-end plain/plain design, how many ends are lifted?
questions.explain: Only the face weave lifts: plain weave raises half of the four face ends, so 2 ends; no back end is lifted.

questions.q: In one 8 × 8 repeat of the plain/plain double cloth (4 face picks and 4 back picks) how many lifted squares are there altogether?
questions.explain: Face picks: 4 × 2 = 8; back picks: 4 × 6 = 24; total 32 of the 64 squares.

questions.q: Ends 1 to 8 are T B T B T B T B. On face pick 1 the face weave lifts ends 1 and 5. Write the row as a two-digit hex number. Take end 1 as the leftmost, most significant bit and 1 = end lifted.

Same design: on back pick 2 every face end (1, 3, 5, 7) is lifted and the back plain weave lifts back ends 2 and 6. Which hex pair writes the row? Take end 1 as the leftmost, most significant bit and 1 = end lifted.
questions.explain: Bits: 1110 1110 → E E. 88 would be a face pick; CC (1100 1100) lifts ends 1, 2, 5, 6, which leaves face ends 3 and 7 down and breaks the rule.

questions.q: A 1:1 double cloth has a plain face and a 2/1 twill back on 12 ends. On a back pick, how many of the 12 ends are lifted?
questions.explain: All 6 face ends are up, and the 2/1 twill lifts 2 of every 3 back ends: 4 of 6. Total 10.

questions.q: A double cloth with a 3/1 twill in both layers is drafted straight. How many healds does it need?
questions.explain: Each 3/1 twill layer needs 4 healds; 4 + 4 = 8.

questions.q: The loom is set with 48 face ends and 48 back ends per inch in a 60-inch reed width. How many ends are in the warp altogether?
questions.explain: Total ends per inch = 96; × 60 inches = 5,760 ends.

questions.q: A plain face and 3/1 twill back, 1:1, are drawn on 16 ends × 16 picks in the lecture. What is the smallest repeat that would also work?
questions.explain: LCM(2, 4) = 4 threads per layer, doubled for two layers = 8; the lecture's 16 × 16 drawing contains two repeats each way.

questions.q: A 3/1 twill in both layers, 1:1, is shown on 16 × 16. How many squares does that drawing contain, and how many of them are face-pick squares?
questions.explain: 16 × 16 = 256 squares; half the picks are face picks, so 8 rows × 16 = 128 squares.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Weaving-shed scenarios: faults, stitching choices and loom requirements for double cloths.

questions.q: A woven double cloth comes off the loom as two loose cloths held together only at the selvedges. What was missing?
questions.explain: The separating lifts worked, but with no stitches the layers form a bag or tube.

questions.q: The back weft shows through on the face of a double cloth in regular spots. What is the most likely cause?
options: Some face ends were left down on a back pick, letting the back weft pass over them
questions.explain: If a face end is not lifted on a back pick the back weft crosses above it and shows on the face; this is the separating rule broken (or an unintended stitch).

questions.q: A stitch placed by lifting a back end on a face pick is visible on the face. How should it be moved?
options: To a position between two face ends that are also lifted on that pick
questions.explain: The lecture's advice: lift the back end where the face ends on either side are up, so they cover it.

questions.q: A heavy blanket is wanted with a smooth plain face and a bulky 3/1 twill back. A loom has 6 healds. Can it weave this double cloth on a straight draft?
options: No: double cloth needs a jacquard
Yes: plain needs 2 and 3/1 twill needs 4, total 6
questions.explain: 2 + 4 = 6 healds, exactly what the loom has.

questions.q: A mill wants to weave a tubular pillowcase in one piece. Which double-cloth construction?
options: Unstitched double cloth, which forms a tube
questions.explain: Left unstitched, the two layers make a tube or bag, which is exactly a seamless pillowcase.

questions.q: Because every face end is lifted on every back pick, the face warp does more bending than a single plain cloth would and its crimp allowance must be checked in costing.
questions.explain: Lifting on a back pick is not an interlacing: the face end simply stays above the back weft. Its crimp comes from the face weave alone, so the usual allowance for that weave applies.

questions.q: A customer wants a reversible fabric with a different colour each side. How does double cloth help?
options: Face and back layers can use different coloured warps and wefts, each weaving its own structure
It cannot; both sides must match
questions.explain: Each layer has its own warp and weft, so the two faces can differ in colour, yarn and weave.

questions.q: A weaver reports the shed is hard to open cleanly on back picks of a plain/plain double cloth. Which fact explains the extra load?
options: On back picks only 2 of every 8 ends are lifted
On back picks 6 of every 8 ends are lifted
questions.explain: All four face ends plus two back ends rise on each back pick, so three-quarters of the warp is lifted, far more than on a face pick.

questions.q: To make a double cloth firmer without visible ties, which change is best?
options: Add stitches by dropping face ends under back picks at points hidden by neighbouring face floats, or add hidden back-end lifts on face picks
Replace the back weave with a long-float satin
questions.explain: Hidden stitching binds the layers while keeping the face clean; removing stitches loosens the cloth.

questions.q: A double cloth made with a 1:1 thread arrangement needs twice the ends per inch in the reed of either layer alone.
questions.explain: Both warps pass through the same reed, so the reed sett is the sum of the face and back setts, twice either one when they are equal.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder questions mixing the separating rule, stitching, hex reading and repeat sizes.

questions.q: Ends 1 to 8 are T B T B T B T B. On back pick 4 all face ends are up and the back plain weave lifts back ends 4 and 8. Which hex pair writes the row? Take end 1 as the leftmost, most significant bit and 1 = end lifted.
questions.explain: Bits: 1011 1011 → B B. EE is the other back pick (back ends 2 and 6 up); 22 is a face pick.

questions.q: Ends 1 to 8 are T B T B T B T B. A row reads hex 22 (0010 0010). Which kind of pick is it?
options: A face pick: only face ends 3 and 7 are up
A back pick: all face ends are up
A back pick with a stitch
questions.explain: Ends 3 and 7 are face ends and no back end is lifted, so this is a face pick of the plain face weave.

questions.q: A row of the 8-end design reads 1110 1110 (hex EE). Which statement is true?
options: It is a back pick: face ends 1, 3, 5, 7 up and back ends 2, 6 up
It is a face pick with four lifts
questions.explain: All four face ends are up and two back ends follow plain weave: a correct back pick with no stitch.

questions.q: A row on a face pick of the 8-end plain/plain design reads 1100 0000 (hex C0). What is wrong with it?
options: Back end 2 is lifted on a face pick, which is either a fault or a stitch not flanked by lifted face ends
Nothing, it is the face weave
questions.explain: Face pick lifts should be face ends only (1 and 5, or 3 and 7). Here end 1 is up but so is end 2, a back end, while end 3 is down, so a stitch there would not be hidden by lifted face ends on both sides.

questions.q: A plain/2-1 twill double cloth repeats on 12 ends × 12 picks (6 face picks, 6 back picks). Face picks lift 3 ends and back picks lift 10. How many lifted squares per repeat?
questions.explain: 6 × 3 = 18 on face picks plus 6 × 10 = 60 on back picks = 78.

questions.q: A designer plans a double cloth with a 5-end sateen face and a plain back, 1:1. What is the minimum ends-repeat?
questions.explain: LCM of 5 and 2 is 10 threads per layer; two layers 1:1 give 20 ends.

questions.q: If a face end is dropped under a back pick as a stitch, the back weft passes over that face end at that point.
questions.explain: Dropping a face end on a back pick lets the back weft cross above it, tying the layers; it must be placed where face floats hide it.

questions.q: A 60-inch warp carries 48 face ends and 48 back ends per inch, with the plain/plain design repeating on 8 ends. How many repeats of the design are there across the width?
questions.explain: Total ends = 96 × 60 = 5,760; ÷ 8 ends per repeat = 720 repeats.

questions.q: Which of these designs would need the most healds on a straight draft?
questions.explain: Add the heald needs of the two layers: 4 + 4 = 8 for twill in both layers, more than 6, 5 or 4.

questions.q: A student draws a double cloth by lifting every back end on every face pick and leaving face ends down on back picks. What results?
options: The layers swap: the intended back becomes the face, but the cloth is still a double cloth
Two layers correctly separated as planned
questions.explain: Reversing the rule consistently simply puts the 'back' layer on top; the structure is still two separate layers, just inverted.
